longForm.title: The Berezina, 1812: Catastrophe and the Miracle Inside It
longForm.excerpt: Between 26 and 29 November 1812, Napoleon's engineers built two bridges across a freezing river and extracted an army from a Russian encirclement. Tens of thousands died. The core of the Grande Armée survived. Both things are true.
paragraphs: The received account of the Berezina — that it was Napoleon's great catastrophe, the moment the Grande Armée finally died — is broadly accurate and substantially wrong about the particulars. The crossing of the Berezina River between 26 and 29 November 1812 was a disaster of the first order. It was also a remarkable operational achievement. That both things are true simultaneously is what makes the Berezina worth examining with some care.

By mid-November 1812, Napoleon had been retreating from Moscow for five weeks. The city he had taken in September had given him nothing: no Russian surrender, no peace negotiation, only a capital the Russians had burned themselves rather than see occupied. The Grande Armée that had crossed into Russia in June — approximately 450,000 strong at the frontier — had been reduced by combat, disease, starvation, and the Russian autumn to somewhere between 80,000 and 100,000 effective troops, trailed by a mass of stragglers, camp followers, and walking wounded that may have added another 30,000 to 40,000 to the column. The question, by November, was not whether Napoleon would retreat but whether his army would exist as an organized force when the retreat ended.

The Russian command had set a trap. The theory was Marshal Kutuzov's, though executing it required cooperation from forces not under his direct command. Admiral Chichagov's Army of the Danube had moved up from the south to hold the western bank of the Berezina at Borisov, cutting the main crossing point on the road to Minsk. General Wittgenstein's corps pressed from the north. Kutuzov's own army followed from the east. The intention was encirclement — a destroying embrace, with the frozen river as the blocking position and three Russian armies as the arms of the pincer. Napoleon, Kutuzov calculated, had no bridging equipment and no way out. What Kutuzov underestimated was Marshal Victor's corps, which Napoleon had maintained as a rearguard in reasonable order, and the emperor's own willingness to improvise under conditions that did not invite improvisation.

The French engineers — the pontonniers of General Jean-Baptiste Eblé — had been ordered to destroy their bridging equipment at Orsha to lighten the army's load. Eblé had retained, against orders and on his own initiative, two field forges, two wagons of charcoal, and six wagons of tools and bridging material. That disobedience almost certainly saved Napoleon's army. When French cavalry seized Borisov from Chichagov's advance guard on November 21, then lost it again the following day, Eblé's men began the work of building new bridges at Studianka, eight miles north of Borisov, where the river was shallower and Chichagov's forces had not yet arrived in strength. They worked in water that was barely above freezing. Contemporary accounts, compiled by historians from soldiers' memoirs and staff reports, describe men standing in ice water for hours at a time, working the trestles by hand, unable to feel their feet. Eblé reportedly walked among them in the water, keeping them moving, knowing that if the work stopped the men would die where they stood.

Two bridges were completed by the morning of November 26 — one for infantry, one for wheeled transport and artillery. The infantry bridge was ready by approximately 1 p.m. The army began to cross. For the organized divisions that went first, the crossing was relatively orderly. Victor's corps held the eastern bank against Wittgenstein. Oudinot and Ney pushed back Chichagov on the western bank. The fighting was severe on both sides, but Napoleon extracted his effective forces intact. By the evening of November 27, most of the surviving combat troops had crossed. What remained on the eastern bank was the mass of stragglers, camp followers, and non-combatants — tens of thousands of people who had traveled with the army and who now could not get across quickly enough.

The disaster that has entered popular memory was what happened to those people. Chichagov's forces were pressing from the south. Victor's rearguard needed to cross. Eblé, who had held the bridges as long as operationally possible, burned them at 9 a.m. on November 29 to prevent Russian capture. The crowds on the eastern bank — estimates range from 10,000 to 40,000, with most historians settling somewhere around 20,000 to 30,000 — were cut off. Many drowned attempting to cross through the ice floes. Many were captured. Many froze in the days that followed. The river itself became a mass grave. When Russian peasants salvaged what they could from the crossing site the following spring, accounts speak of bodies emerging from the ice for miles downstream.

The historiographical debate has turned, over the past two decades, on the question of who bears responsibility for the catastrophe among the stragglers. The standard 19th-century French account — still partly visible in early 20th-century military histories — blamed the stragglers themselves: they had been warned, they had delayed, and their deaths were the consequence of disorder rather than policy. Adam Zamoyski, in his 2004 study of the campaign, pushed back against this framing methodically and without sentimentality. The people who died at the Berezina were in most cases camp followers who had no alternative to traveling with the army. They did not delay crossing out of disorder; they delayed because the bridges were bottlenecked and armed soldiers had priority. The army's survival required their abandonment. This does not mean Napoleon planned their deaths. It means the operational logic of the crossing demanded it, and the army acted accordingly.

What the French army lost at the Berezina in terms of combat effectiveness is harder to quantify than it might appear. The fighting units that crossed were badly understrength — some regiments numbered in the hundreds rather than thousands — but they were organized, armed, and under command. The corps structure survived. The officer cadre, which took years to train and could not be replaced quickly, came through in substantial numbers. Napoleon would fight on for two more years with these men as his nucleus. The 1813 campaign across Saxony, prosecuted by the survivors of 1812 and ending in the catastrophe at Leipzig, demonstrated that the French army remained a capable force even after everything the Russian campaign had cost it. That was not what Kutuzov had intended.

Jean-Baptiste Eblé died of exhaustion and exposure on December 31, 1812, less than five weeks after his engineers finished burning the bridges he had built against orders to save the army. Napoleon is said to have mourned him. The pontonniers who worked in the ice water at Studianka are not individually commemorated. The mathematics of memory work like the mathematics of everything else: it is easier to count the dead than to name the people who prevented more of them. The Berezina was a catastrophe. It was also the reason approximately 80,000 Frenchmen made it home.

shortForm.title: The Pusan Perimeter, 1950: Stand or Die
shortForm.excerpt: By August 1950, UN forces had been driven to a 140-mile defensive line in Korea's southeastern corner. Walton Walker's order was unambiguous. The perimeter held for two months until MacArthur's Inchon landing made it irrelevant.
paragraphs: By early August 1950, the United States Eighth Army and the Republic of Korea's battered divisions had been driven into a perimeter roughly 140 miles long and 50 miles wide at the southeastern corner of the Korean peninsula, anchored on the port of Pusan. The North Korean People's Army had crossed the 38th Parallel on June 25, overrun Seoul within three days, and driven south with a speed that confounded American planning assumptions. Task Force Smith — the first American ground unit committed to battle — was overwhelmed at Osan on July 5. What followed was a fighting retreat that covered two hundred miles in five weeks and came close to collapsing the entire UN commitment to Korea.

Lieutenant General Walton Walker, commanding the Eighth Army, issued what military historians have called the 'stand or die' order on July 29. It was blunter in its original form than the name suggests: Walker told his commanders there would be no more withdrawals, no 'Dunkirk' evacuation, and that a final beachhead would not be established. Whether he used the words 'stand or die' specifically has been contested — the order's exact language varies across accounts — but the intent was clear. The Naktong River formed the western and northern boundary of the perimeter. Behind it, Walker positioned what remained of his army and the ROK divisions along a line that contracted and expanded over the summer as North Korean offensives broke through and counterattacks restored it.

The two months of fighting around the Pusan Perimeter produced battles that have not entered the popular memory of the Korean War in proportion to their severity. The First and Second Battles of the Naktong Bulge, in August and September, saw the 24th Infantry Division and the 1st Marine Provisional Brigade fighting NKPA formations that crossed the river on rafts and by wading. In early September, the NKPA launched what it called its Great Naktong Offensive — a coordinated assault across the entire front timed to break through before UN reinforcements could arrive in sufficient strength. Walker's forces held, barely, at a cost that depleted both sides. The Eighth Army at this point was receiving replacements almost as fast as it was taking losses.

The perimeter was relieved not by a frontal breakthrough but by MacArthur's landing at Inchon on September 15, which cut NKPA supply lines and forced a general retreat. The defenders of the Pusan Perimeter are rarely examined in isolation from the landing that ended their ordeal, but the historical case is clear: had the perimeter collapsed in August or early September, the strategic position in Korea would have been unrecoverable on any timeline that mattered. Walker's insistence on holding a compact, defensible line and feeding reserves to threatened points rather than attempting a general counteroffensive was operationally sound and, as events proved, sufficient. He died in a jeep accident on December 23, 1950, before the war ended and before the battles he fought were properly assessed.

onThisDay.headline: Napoleon Arrives at Elba After Abdication
onThisDay.summary: On 4 May 1814, Napoleon Bonaparte arrived at the island of Elba in the Mediterranean, beginning his first exile after abdicating the French imperial throne on April 11. The Treaty of Fontainebleau had assigned him nominal sovereignty over the island, a small guard, and an annual pension. He would remain less than ten months before departing for France on February 26, 1815, beginning the Hundred Days.
